title: Human Reproduction: Gametogenesis, Menstrual Cycle and Development
subcategory: Human Reproduction — Reproductive Systems, Gametogenesis, Fertilisation, Pregnancy
summary: Human reproduction is sexual and viviparous: gametogenesis produces haploid sperm and ova in the primary sex organs, the menstrual cycle prepares the female reproductive tract for a potential pregnancy each month, and after internal fertilisation the zygote implants and develops through a placenta-supported pregnancy ending in parturition and lactation.
explanation: SPERMATOGENESIS occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testis: a diploid spermatogonium undergoes mitotic multiplication, then one primary spermatocyte enters meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes (haploid, still with duplicated chromatids), which complete meiosis II to give four haploid spermatids; spermiogenesis then transforms spermatids into motile spermatozoa (each with an acrosome-capped head, midpiece packed with mitochondria for ATP, and a flagellum for motility). Sertoli cells nourish developing sperm and are regulated by FSH; Leydig cells (interstitial) secrete testosterone under LH stimulation. OOGENESIS begins in FETAL life: oogonia multiply and enter meiosis I but arrest at prophase I as primary oocytes (contained in primordial follicles) until puberty. Each month, one primary oocyte resumes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte (large, retaining nearly all the cytoplasm) and a much smaller first polar body — the UNEQUAL cytoplasmic division ensures the future egg has enough reserves to support early development. The secondary oocyte arrests again at METAPHASE II and is released at ovulation; meiosis II is completed only IF fertilisation occurs, yielding the ovum and a second polar body. The MENSTRUAL CYCLE (~28 days) has three phases driven by the hypothalamus-pituitary-ovary-uterus axis: the MENSTRUAL phase (endometrium sheds, ~day 1-5, if no implantation occurred), the FOLLICULAR/PROLIFERATIVE phase (FSH drives follicle growth; the growing follicle secretes rising estrogen, which thickens the endometrium and triggers a LH surge around day 14), and the LUTEAL/SECRETORY phase (the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium and prepares it for implantation; if no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and menstruation begins the next cycle). FERTILISATION normally occurs in the AMPULLA of the fallopian tube: a sperm penetrates the corona radiata and zona pellucida, triggering the acrosome reaction and, after fusion, a cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy (fertilisation by more than one sperm). The resulting diploid zygote undergoes rapid mitotic cleavage as it travels toward the uterus, forming a morula and then a blastocyst (with an inner cell mass that becomes the embryo and an outer trophoblast that implants into the endometrium ~day 6-7). The placenta, formed from both trophoblast (fetal) and endometrial (maternal) tissue, is the site of nutrient/gas/waste exchange (via diffusion, NOT direct blood mixing) and also functions as an endocrine gland, secreting hCG (maintains the corpus luteum early in pregnancy — the hormone detected by pregnancy tests), estrogen, progesterone, and hPL. PARTURITION (childbirth) is triggered by neuroendocrine signals near full term, culminating in a positive-feedback loop of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causing increasingly strong uterine (myometrial) contractions. LACTATION is stimulated by prolactin (milk production) and oxytocin (milk ejection reflex, triggered by suckling); colostrum, the first milk, is especially rich in antibodies (IgA) that provide passive immunity to the newborn.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking oogenesis and spermatogenesis both produce four functional gametes per meiosis — spermatogenesis does, but oogenesis produces only ONE functional ovum plus polar bodies, due to highly unequal cytoplasmic division.
Assuming maternal and fetal blood mix directly in the placenta — the two circulations remain separate, with exchange occurring across a thin diffusion barrier, not by direct blood mixing.

Believing meiosis II in the female is complete before ovulation — the secondary oocyte is actually arrested at metaphase II and is released in that state; meiosis II only completes if a sperm fertilises it.
examples: A home pregnancy test detects hCG in urine — this hormone is secreted by the developing placenta specifically to keep the corpus luteum (and hence progesterone secretion) active until the placenta itself takes over hormone production.
Colostrum given to a newborn in the first few days provides passive immunity via IgA antibodies, before the infant's own adaptive immune system has had time to develop its own antibody responses.
genZNote: Oogenesis: nature's ultimate 'keep the loot, ditch the roommate' — the egg hoards nearly all the cytoplasm, the polar bodies get evicted.
